metadata.title: Climate Tech Is Everywhere: AI Meets Every Industry
metadata.audience: students: smart people getting started with AI
metadata.structure_note: User script is the whole narration to stay under 3:00; composer cold open and hesitant-writer overview omitted on purpose. Closing question = Your Turn beat.
metadata.reformat: full-length; native portrait graphics; preserve source framing

beats.narration_text: Imagine waking up in a city where your coffee was grown using less water, your electricity came from a smarter energy grid, your building adjusted itself to the weather, and your clothes were manufactured with less pollution.

qc.sparse_reason: build-up beat: the four morning cards land one per phrase; mid-beat frames show the partial row

beats.narration_text: What if all of these seemingly unrelated things had one thing in common? Climate technology.

show.event: four icons around an empty center
lines draw to the center; 'Climate technology' lands

beats.narration_text: When we think about climate tech, we often picture electric vehicles, solar panels, or wind turbines. But climate change touches almost every industry, from agriculture and transportation to construction, manufacturing, fashion, and even the way we manage waste.

show.event: three familiar chips: EVs, solar, wind

beats.narration_text: The challenge isn't just inventing cleaner technologies. It's making entire systems more efficient, less resource-intensive, and capable of adapting to a changing climate.

show.event: three system goals land in order

shot.visual_intent: Better systems, not just new tech.

qc.sparse_reason: build-up beat: old framing, label, then three goal cards land one per phrase

beats.narration_text: And this is where STEM comes in. Science helps us understand how the climate, materials, water, and ecosystems behave. Engineering turns that knowledge into solutions, from designing energy-efficient buildings to developing cleaner manufacturing processes.

Mathematics helps us quantify emissions, energy demand, water use, and environmental risk. And technology allows us to collect and analyze information at a scale that would otherwise be impossible. But what happens when we add artificial intelligence to all of this?
AI can help farmers predict crop stress using weather and soil data. It can help energy grids balance electricity demand with fluctuating renewable energy supplies.

show.event: farm panel: plants with stress bars; one flagged
grid panel: wavy supply meets steady demand

qc.sparse_reason: build-up beat: farm panel first, the grid panel lands at the second sentence

beats.narration_text: In buildings, it can predict energy needs and optimize heating and cooling. In manufacturing, it can detect inefficiencies, reduce material waste, and identify opportunities to reuse resources.

show.event: factory panel: waste bar shrinks, reuse loop

qc.sparse_reason: build-up beat: buildings panel first, the manufacturing panel lands at the second sentence

beats.narration_text: AI doesn't replace climate scientists or engineers. It gives them another tool to understand complex systems, make better decisions, and potentially act faster.

show.event: scientists + engineers cards, AI added as a tool

qc.sparse_reason: build-up beat: the three steps land one per phrase

beats.narration_text: The real opportunity isn't just making AI smarter. It's using intelligence to make the systems we depend on smarter, cleaner, and more resilient.

qc.sparse_reason: build-up beat: the old framing, then the new one, then three chips land; mid-beat frames show the partial build

beats.narration_text: So here's a question: If AI can help optimize almost every industry, which industry do you think has the greatest opportunity to make a meaningful difference for our climate?
